title: One human race
hook: recognize all humankind as one (Akal Ustat 85)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akal Ustat, the poem that walks past kings and pilgrims and says the Lord is found by love. Your line was praise of the timeless. What did you put back in scale? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

Forms ask. Box one, box two, box three. Religion, caste, nationality, community. Hospital intake sheets, school applications, a matchmaker's questions over chai. Sometimes the boxes are there to help. Sometimes they decide who sits where, who marries whom, who drinks from which well. The tenth Guru lived in a world full of such boxes, and in one stanza of Akal Ustat he lists them, one by one, and then picks up the very word the boxes were built on and gives it to everyone.
screen: `BOX ONE, BOX TWO, BOX THREE.` → `WHO SITS WHERE.` → `HE TAKES THE BOX WORD.`

segments.voice: Here is the stanza, in paraphrase. Someone has become a shaven-headed renouncer; someone a yogi; someone a celibate student; someone an ascetic. Some are Hindus, some Muslims; some are Shia, some Sunni. Then the line Sikhs quote today: recognize the whole human race as one. In Gurmukhi, manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo. Look at the word jat. In everyday speech it's the word for caste, the box you're born into, the one that decided so much. The Guru keeps the word and widens it until it holds everyone. There is one jat, and it is the human one. Notice also the verb: pahichanbo, recognize. He doesn't say make everyone one, or pretend the labels aren't there. He has just named the renouncer, the yogi, the Hindu, the Muslim. The labels are real. The call is to recognize what's under them. The stanza then turns toward God, again in paraphrase: the Creator and the Merciful are the same; the Provider and the Compassionate are the same; there is no difference, and to think there is, is error. He uses names for God from more than one language, side by side, and says they point to one. In the Sikh tradition this line isn't a slogan on a wall. It sits beside langar, where anyone eats sitting in the same row, and beside the gurdwara's open doors. A teaching about recognition, practiced with a plate and a floor. It doesn't ask anyone to stop being who they are. It asks them to see one family when they look around the room.
screen: `RENOUNCER, YOGI, HINDU, MUSLIM.` · `ONE JAT: THE HUMAN ONE.` · `RECOGNIZE, NOT ERASE.` · `CREATOR AND MERCIFUL, THE SAME.` · then, large: `ONE HUMAN RACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat everyone as family today, starting now. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you'll pass today: a driver, a cashier, a coworker you find hard, someone in a uniform, someone whose head covering differs from yours, or who wears none. Take them one at a time. Notice the box your mind puts each one in, quickly, without scolding yourself. Then, on the out-breath, say inwardly: family. Just that one word for each of them. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between faces. The bell holds the time.
One human race. Manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo: recognize the whole human race as one, the tenth Guru's line in Akal Ustat. Today's word.
Your line: one human race. Today, greet one stranger the way you'd greet a cousin at a family wedding. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs quote 'manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo' from Akal Ustat when speaking about equality, and it is lived out in langar, where everyone eats together seated in the same rows.

match.prompt: the stanza, piece by piece: tap the pairs.
pairs: the line lived with a plate

myth: the stanza says labels like Hindu and Muslim aren't real
it names them, then asks us to recognize the one human race beneath them.
the Guru uses the word for caste to name all humanity
manas ki jat: the human jat, one for everyone.
the stanza says the different names for God point to different gods
Creator and Merciful, Provider and Compassionate: the same, it says.

fork.setup: you're the Guru, and you've just listed renouncers, yogis, Hindus, Muslims, Shia and Sunni. what's the next line?
options: tell them to drop their labels.
say one group has it right.
recognize the whole human race as one.
fork.reveal: manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo: recognize, not erase, and rank no one.

original.script: ਮਾਨਸ ਕੀ ਜਾਤਿ ਸਬੈ ਏਕੈ ਪਹਿਚਾਨਬੋ
original.say: MAA-nus kee JAAT sa-BAI AY-kai peh-CHAAN-bo
original.note: recognize the whole human race as one: jat, the word for caste, made wide enough for all.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'one human race' is a modern slogan.
what it means: the tenth Guru's line in Akal Ustat: recognize the whole human race as one.
what a scholar hears: he uses jat, the word for caste, and the verb is recognize, not erase.

sources.ref: Dasam Granth, Akal Ustat 85 (koi bhaio mundia sanniasi ... manas ki jat sabhai ekai pahichanbo ... karta karim soi)

notes: The stanza is paraphrased from memory; please check the list of renouncers and groups (mundia sanniasi, jogi, brahmachari, jati, Hindu, Turk, Rafzi, Imam Shafi) and the gloss of Rafzi/Imam Shafi as Shia/Sunni.
The gloss of jat as the everyday word for caste is a meaning gloss, not an etymology; please confirm.
Transliteration and Gurmukhi of the line (ਮਾਨਸ ਕੀ ਜਾਤਿ ਸਬੈ ਏਕੈ ਪਹਿਚਾਨਬੋ) and the pronunciation guide should be checked.
The link to langar is a teaching connection, not a claim made by the stanza; please confirm it is fair.
